name: Howard Lutnick
role: U.S. Secretary of Commerce (since February 2025); former chairman and CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald
summary: Howard Lutnick promoted protective tariffs and domestic manufacturing as U.S. commerce secretary. He negotiated a strategic investment programme with Japan and backed federal investment in semiconductor manufacturing and new nuclear capacity. He advocates cutting federal deficits and selecting immigrants for their economic contribution.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Lutnick’s growth plan calls for the Federal Reserve to continue setting policy rates, with a new chair who would cut them.

abolish-ip.rationale: Lutnick told the Senate he wanted to improve access to patents, reduce the application backlog and protect American patent and trademark holders from abuse of the system.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: No recorded position found on a future society without money.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Lutnick called for stablecoin issuers to help law enforcement trace illicit transactions. His testimony leaves open whether people should retain access to another untraceable means of payment.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Lutnick called the roughly $2 trillion 2021 rescue package unnecessary and blamed it for inflation. He later made ending persistent federal deficits a stated goal of his economic programme.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Lutnick called for a Fed chair who would lower rates. His preferred appointment and rate outcome leave open whether elected officials should have authority over the Fed’s decisions.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Lutnick argued for drilling to lower energy prices in September 2024 and subsequently reiterated the case for developing U.S. natural gas resources at the Pennsylvania energy summit.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Lutnick signed the strategic investment agreement with Japan and chaired its investment committee. The two governments then named the construction of small modular reactors in Tennessee and Alabama for joint support under the agreement.

free-trade.rationale: Lutnick argued that the postwar reduction of trade protection weakened U.S. industry after its original purpose of reconstruction had ended. He described NAFTA as a lasting blow to the economic prospects of U.S. manufacturing communities.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: Lutnick defended raising cattle for food and advocated opening overseas markets to American ranchers’ beef.

limit-growth.rationale: Lutnick promoted rapid growth and opposed specific rules affecting mining and energy. His remarks leave open whether to accept slower growth when environmental protection requires it.

nation-first.rationale: Lutnick recommended maintaining duties even on shipments from trading partners when he judged import dependence a threat to American copper production and national security.

no-central-bank.rationale: Lutnick called for a new Federal Reserve chair who would lower policy rates as part of his plan to reach faster growth. His proposal assigns an active monetary policy role to the Fed.

open-borders.rationale: Lutnick argued that the United States should keep its borders controlled while providing public benefits and should grant admission selectively where it sees a clear benefit to the country.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: Lutnick presented eliminating federal debt as a desirable endpoint for Gold Card revenue and emphasized the resulting savings on annual interest payments.

private-courts-defense.rationale: No recorded position found on replacing public courts with private companies.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Lutnick supports screening immigrants for economic contribution and giving preference to high earners. His proposed selection criteria leave the total level of immigration open.

regulate-corporations.rationale: In public statements reproduced in his Senate questionnaire, Lutnick advocated reducing regulation across the economy alongside lowering taxes to bring businesses back to the United States.

restrict-technology-exports-to-rivals.rationale: Commerce under Lutnick required licenses for previously exempt semiconductor manufacturing exports to China and established conditions for sales of certain advanced chips. Lutnick reportedly delayed additional restrictions on suspected intermediaries, leaving a record of selective controls.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Lutnick said he judges his work as secretary by outcomes and described checking a contract for compliance in place of discarding it on partisan grounds.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Asked whether presidential orders could override the statutory authority of the Minority Business Development Agency, Lutnick said he would carry them out to the extent permitted by law.

state-as-business.rationale: Lutnick said he took the same focus on results into the Commerce Department that he had used as a business executive and evaluated public spending by whether it delivered value to taxpayers.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Lutnick signed the Japan agreement creating a committee chaired by the Commerce Secretary to direct investment to priority industries. The Intel agreement also redirected federal semiconductor grants into an $8.9 billion equity investment.

state-harmful.rationale: Lutnick defended the role of the U.S. government in maintaining a court system that protects businesses and in financing infrastructure and public retirement benefits.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Lutnick’s Section 232 report recommended an immediate 30 percent tariff on semi-finished copper products and phased duties on refined copper to preserve domestic production capacity.

territorial-expansion.rationale: His discussion of the Panama Canal concerned oversight of the waterway, and his comments on Greenland addressed a particular possible accession with local consent. His general position on territorial expansion remains open.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Lutnick used benefit costs to argue for selective admission. His remarks leave open whether permanent residents already living in the country should be eligible for welfare.

notes: This pass checked the Senate nomination hearing and written answers, later Commerce appropriations testimony, trade and investment records, and long-form interviews. Follow-up research covered elections, statutory and judicial limits, federal and state authority, war and alliances, Greenland and the Panama Canal, race and sex equality, marriage, abortion, religion, climate, energy, trade, welfare, and technology. The local congressional-hearing index, MediaSum interviews and reference library were checked. Economic and trade positions make up most of the recorded answers. His descriptions of being socially liberal and fiscally conservative were used to find sources on individual issues. The nomination questionnaire also reproduces his earlier public posts. The first-hand rally remarks were checked in the full event transcript.
